rules.message: Hardcoded secret-shaped literal (an API-key/password/token assignment, or a known cloud-key prefix) — a credential committed to source is exposed to every reader/fork/clone and cannot be rotated without a code change. Move it to an environment variable or a secrets manager (e.g. `process.env.API_KEY`, or `std::env::var` in Rust) — but that only stops the NEXT leak: this value is already exposed via git history and any forks/clones that pulled it, so rotate/revoke the actual credential too. The match is NOT on the property name alone — a VALUE-SHAPE gate rejects identifier-shaped values: any literal built from letter-only words joined by `-`/`_` (`"mantine-DatePickerInput-input"`, `"refresh-token"`, `"MY_API_KEY"`) is a CSS class / selector / constant name, not a credential, and is dropped in any casing. That CASING-AGNOSTIC arm belongs to THIS rule only: the sibling CRITICAL rule `security/jwt-sign-literal-secret` keeps just the all-lowercase `snake_case`/`kebab-case` arms (the `UPPER_SNAKE` and `PascalCase` shapes are dropped by both), so a MIXED-CASE identifier-shaped value is silent here and still fires there — `apiKey: "Mantine_DatePicker_Input"` reports nothing while `jwt.sign(payload, "Mantine_DatePicker_Input")` on the next line reports a critical. That split is deliberate, not drift: the false positives that widened this veto were all measured on the `key: value` assignment shape, none on the positional `jwt.sign` shape, and widening a CRITICAL rule's veto with no measurement behind it buys silence, not signal. Measured on the corpus that motivated the gate (all seven findings came from one `ALLOW` table in a lint script): SIX of the seven are dropped by it. The seventh, `token: "adsbygoogle"`, is a separator-free single word and DELIBERATELY still fires — no shape test tells it apart from a weak literal password like `token: "letmeinplease"`, and silencing the one would silence the other. A value whose segments carry digits keeps firing (`"sk-a1B2c3D4e5F6g7H8i9J0"`), as does a separator-free word (`"Changemeplease"`), so weak literal passwords are not silenced. Blind spot, measured rather than guessed: this is a SHAPE test, not entropy, so a passphrase-style credential built from dictionary words (`"correct-horse-battery-staple"`, `"trombone_ravine_wallet_ember"`) is ALWAYS silenced, and a random base64url token is silenced whenever it happens to draw no digits — about 0.9% of 24-char, 0.26% of 32-char and 0.04% of 43-char tokens (200k samples each). Nothing is lost for base64-standard, hex or alphanumeric values (0%, those alphabets carry no `-`/`_`), and every common vendor prefix keeps firing (AWS `AKIA…`, `sk_live_…`, `ghp_…`, `xoxb-…`). Shape remains THIS rule's ceiling, but it is no longer the analysis's: the string-literal-with-binding-name IR node this sentence used to ask for now exists, and the sibling rule `security/high-entropy-secret` reads it — both silenced classes fire there when the value clears a measured 80-total-Shannon-bit floor and the binding name ends in a secret keyword, with the value itself never stored (hash + entropy only). Still silent in BOTH rules, stated so the pair is not mistaken for closure: sub-floor passphrases (88.5% of 3-word phrases measure under 80 bits), and any secret whose binding name matches neither vocabulary. The `assignment` arm needs the value to follow the NAME directly, which Rust's typed form does not do (`const API_KEY: &str = "…"` puts a type in between), so a second `rust-str-const` arm keyed on `: &str =` covers exactly that shape — a `const`/`static` of any OTHER type, and a `let` binding with an explicit type, are not matched by it (the untyped `let api_key = "…"` still goes through the `assignment` arm). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-hardcoded-secret-ok`.

High-entropy string literal bound to a secret-named binding (name ending in api-key/apikey/secret/passwd/password/token) — a credential committed to source is exposed to every reader/fork/clone and cannot be rotated without a code change; rotate/revoke the actual credential, then move the replacement to an environment variable or a secrets manager. This rule reads the string-literal-with-binding-name IR node (name + value hash + value entropy, NEVER the value itself — nothing secret-shaped is written to the analysis cache), which is exactly the fix `hardcoded-secret`'s message used to name as its own ceiling: that line scan's identifier-shape veto killed a dictionary-word passphrase (`"correct-horse-battery-staple"`, 97.9 total Shannon bits) identically to a CSS class name, and killed a random base64url token whenever it drew no digits. The judgment here is MEASURED ENTROPY, not value shape: total Shannon bits over the value's bytes, threshold 80 (measured separation, 2026-08-03: 4-word passphrases p5 = 83.0 so 2.9% are missed; 24-char no-digit base64url tokens floor = 85.0 so 0% missed; the hardest true negatives sit below — `"PlaceholderSecretValue"` 75.7, `"a7Fk29QmZx41Lp08Wd"` 75.1, `"refresh_token"` 41.4). Three vetoes, each stated with what it cannot do: a value LITERALLY equal to its own binding name is dropped by hash equality (`refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — exact equality only, a hash cannot case-fold); a mock/test/fake/dummy/sample/placeholder/example word in the binding NAME is dropped, boundary-anchored (name start, `-`/`_`, digit, or a camelCase transition — `mockApiKey`/`test_secret`/`myTestToken` are vetoed; `latestToken`/`attestationSecret`, which merely EMBED `test`, keep firing); but a placeholder word in the VALUE is invisible by design — a value-side veto is structurally impossible here because the channel never carries the value (it is reduced to hash + entropy at extraction, the same choice that keeps candidate secrets out of the plain-text cache) — so a long placeholder or i18n value bound to a clean secret name relies on sitting under the 80-bit floor, and one that clears it fires. Remaining blindness, measured rather than guessed: a WEAK sub-floor credential (`password`, `admin123456`) never reaches this rule — a short or low-diversity string sits under any useful floor by construction, and that class is the sibling `hardcoded-secret` line scan's to catch; an English-word identifier chain long enough to clear the floor (`"mantine-DatePickerInput-input"`, 107.4 bits) is indistinguishable from a passphrase by any content-free statistic, so when bound to a secret-ending name it fires — that direction (noise on secret-named bindings) is chosen over the old silence; and 3-word passphrases mostly sit under the floor (88.5% below 80) — a floor low enough to catch them would swallow the placeholder negatives above. Digit-carrying values and known vendor prefixes are `hardcoded-secret`'s (unchanged) line-scan business, so one committed `sk_live_…` can legitimately carry both findings. This rule fires only in languages whose parser projects the channel (TS/JS, Python, Java, C#, Go, Rust — silence elsewhere is no-evidence, never clean), and scans test regions (a committed fixture credential still has to be rotated). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-high-entropy-secret-ok` (`#` comments work too).

A high-entropy secret value is committed in a configuration file (`jwt.secret`, `*.password`, `api-key`, ... in a config file — `.properties`, `.ya?ml`, `.toml`, `.ini`, `.conf`, `.cfg`, or `.env`) — this is a live credential exposed to every reader/fork/clone AND preserved in git history, and unlike a code literal it is often the app's real signing key or datastore password. Move it to an environment variable or secrets manager referenced from config (`jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET}`) AND rotate/revoke the committed value. An empty value, a short placeholder (<16 chars), and a `${VAR}` env reference are not flagged. Suppress a vetted case with `# zzop-config-file-secret-ok`.

A secret-shaped query parameter (`api_key`/`access_token`/`token`/`secret`) appears in a URL — URLs are logged by proxies, load balancers, browser history and the `Referer` header. Move the credential into an `Authorization` header (or body/cookie) instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-api-key-in-url-ok`.

A server-only-shaped env var (`SECRET`/`PRIVATE`/`SERVICE_ROLE`/`SERVICE_KEY`) is referenced from frontend code — build tools inline `process.env.*`/`import.meta.env.*` into the shipped JS bundle, making it readable in devtools. PATH SCOPE, disclosed because a security rule's silence reads as a clean bill of health when it is not one: "frontend code" here means exactly two things — ANY `.tsx`/`.jsx` file anywhere in the tree, or a `.ts`/`.js` file under a path segment literally named `fe`, `frontend`, `client` or `web`. A plain `.ts`/`.js` module that is nonetheless bundled into the client (`src/lib/api.ts` in a Next.js app, a `shared/`/`common/` helper, a non-`.tsx` file under `app/`/`pages/`/`components/`) is never scanned, and `.mjs`/`.cjs` are not scanned at all. A `process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in `src/lib/api.ts` is therefore invisible here: zero findings from this rule means "not scanned there", never "no server-only secret reaches the bundle". If the value is genuinely secret, the only correct fix is moving its use behind a backend endpoint (proxy it server-side) — do not just rename it with a `NEXT_PUBLIC_`/`VITE_` prefix. Only reach for that prefix if the value was never actually secret to begin with (e.g. a public config flag flagged by mistake). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-secret-env-in-fe-ok`.

A password-shaped literal is hardcoded — a direct assignment (`password = "..."`) or a JDBC `getConnection(url, user, password)` call with literal credentials — exposed to every reader of the repo and impossible to rotate without a code change. Read it from an environment variable, an excluded properties file, or a secrets manager — but that only stops the NEXT leak: this password is already exposed via git history and any forks/clones that pulled it, so rotate/revoke the actual credential too. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-hardcoded-password-ok`.

A connection-string URL embeds a password directly in source (`scheme://user:pass@host`) — anyone with repo read access effectively owns the datastore, and git history preserves the credential even after it's later removed from HEAD. Move the URL to environment/secret configuration AND rotate the credential (treat it as already compromised). An INTERPOLATED userinfo slot is not flagged, in every language this rule scans: a `${...}` template placeholder, a `{{...}}`/`<...>` template hole, a `process.env` read, or a Rust `format!`/`write!` placeholder (`{}`, `{name}`, `{0}`) sitting between `://` and `@` means the password is not in this source line at all — there is nothing here to rotate, and saying otherwise would send a reader chasing a credential that does not exist. That veto stays anchored to the userinfo slot: a placeholder in the HOST slot does not launder a password spelled literally before the `@`. Loopback hosts (localhost/127.0.0.1) and placeholder-shaped passwords (`changeme`, `mypwd`, ...) are not flagged; suppress a remaining vetted sample with `// zzop-conn-string-credentials-ok`.

A PEM-format private key (a `-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----` header carrying its base64 key body, or a header alone on a dedicated key line) is committed to source — header-plus-key-material is unambiguous, so unlike a heuristic secret-shaped literal there's no plausible non-key reading of this text (a prose mention of the header in docs/i18n strings, with no base64 body accompanying it, does NOT fire). The moment this repo is shared (a fork, a clone, a public push) the key is compromised, and git history keeps it even after the file is later removed. Rotate the key immediately and move it to a secret store (a vault, KMS, or CI secret) instead — an actual PEM header sitting in a test fixture is still a committed key, so this rule scans test paths too, not just application code. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a throwaway key generated only for a test, never used against a real service) with `// zzop-private-key-committed-ok`.

A live-mode vendor credential appears in its recognized production-token format — Stripe `sk_live_`/`rk_live_`, a GitHub `ghp_`/`gho_` personal access token, a Slack `xox[bpars]-` token, or a Google API key (`AIza...`). Format alone identifies these as production secrets, and a committed credential is a leaked credential the instant the repo is shared, regardless of later git-history cleanup. Deliberately NOT matched: Stripe `sk_test_...` — a test-mode key is not a production credential, so flagging it would be noise, not signal. Rotate the credential through the vendor's own key-rotation/revocation flow immediately, then move the replacement into env/secret storage. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-vendor-token-committed-ok`.

`jwt.sign(payload, "...")` is called with a positional string-literal signing secret — anyone who reads this line can forge a validly-signed token for any payload they want. This is a distinct shape from `hardcoded-secret`: that rule's `assignment` pattern needs a `key: value`/`key = value` shape, so a positional literal passed straight as `jwt.sign`'s second argument is uncovered by it — this rule closes that gap. Their identifier-shaped-VALUE vetoes diverge too, and this one is deliberately NARROWER: this rule drops only all-lowercase `snake_case`/`kebab-case` values (plus the `UPPER_SNAKE`/`PascalCase` shapes both rules drop), while `hardcoded-secret` drops letter-only words joined by `-`/`_` in ANY casing. So a mixed-case value such as `"Mantine_DatePicker_Input"` is silenced as a CSS-class/constant name there and still fires here — on purpose: the false positives that widened the sibling's veto were all measured on the `key: value` shape, no measurement has arrived for this positional form, and an identifier-shaped signing key is still a forgeable signing key. Move the signing secret into an environment variable or secrets manager, and rotate the exposed key (it's already leaked via git history and any forks/clones that pulled it). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-jwt-sign-literal-secret-ok`.

`$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe` called — these run the given SQL as-is with no parameterization, so any request-derived string interpolated into it is a SQL injection. Use `$queryRaw`/`$executeRaw` tagged templates (or pass values as separate arguments) so Prisma parameterizes the query. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-raw-query-unsafe-api-ok`.

JPA `@Query` built via string concatenation (`@Query("..." + ...)`). INJECTION IS NOT THE RISK HERE, and the `info` severity is deliberate, not an under-call: Java requires every annotation element value to be a CONSTANT EXPRESSION (JLS 9.7.1), so the concatenated operand is a literal or a `static final` constant the COMPILER folds in place — code that would splice a request-derived value into an annotation does not compile at all (even a `static final` initialized from `System.getenv(...)` is not a constant variable and is rejected at the annotation site). So there is no injection path to analyze in this position, by language rule rather than by the limits of this matcher — do not re-escalate this rule on the theory that better annotation parsing would find one. What remains is hygiene: a concatenated `@Query` hides the full statement from review and makes future refactors error-prone. Prefer a single literal, with named parameters (`:param` with `@Param`) for values. The RUNTIME sibling `security/sql-string-concat` is the injectable shape — string concatenation in ordinary code, where nothing constrains the operand to a constant — and it keeps its higher severity for exactly that reason. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-annotation-sql-concat-ok`.

A SQL string is built by concatenating an expression into the statement text — if the concatenated part is request-derived, this is SQL injection (the input rewrites the query); even a constant fragment hides that risk from review. Use a parameterized/bound query instead (PreparedStatement `?`, JPA `:named` + setParameter) — never escape values into the string. Annotation lines are excluded — element values are compile-time constants (JLS 9.7.1), so the request-derived claim above is structurally false there, and `annotation-sql-concat` owns that shape at info. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-sql-string-concat-ok`.

A SQL statement is assembled by a Rust `format!`/`write!`/`writeln!` macro whose template carries a `{...}` placeholder — the interpolated value becomes part of the statement TEXT, so if it is request-derived this is SQL injection, and even a constant fragment hides that risk from review. Bind the value as a query PARAMETER instead (the driver's `$1`/`?` placeholder plus a bound argument) and keep the statement text a constant. What is matched is a SHAPE, not a dataflow: the template literal IS the statement — it begins (leading whitespace aside) with `SELECT ... FROM` / `DELETE FROM` / `INSERT INTO` / `MERGE INTO` / `UPDATE ... SET` — and carries a `{` placeholder ANYWHERE in it, on EITHER side of the statement keywords: `format!("SELECT {} FROM users", cols)` (a dynamic column list, the classic non-parameterizable vector) and `format!("SELECT * FROM {}", table)` fire exactly as `format!("... WHERE name = '{}'", name)` does. It does NOT prove the interpolated expression is untrusted, which is why this is `warning` and not `critical` — the same standing the Java sibling `security/sql-string-concat` takes for `"..." + ident`. A literal that merely MENTIONS a statement keyword mid-sentence is not matched: `format!("failed to DELETE FROM cache for key {}", key)` is a log line, not a statement text, and the begins-with-a-statement anchor is what keeps it silent — the disclosed cost of that anchor is that a template carrying prose BEFORE a real statement is missed. The statement keywords are UPPERCASE ONLY, and that is the other half of the same precision gate, not an oversight — the call `sql/raw-sql-check-then-write` already makes, for the same reason: `format!("Select {} from the list of available regions", choice)` is English prose that is ALSO a syntactically valid `SELECT <col> FROM <table> ...` head (`format!("Update {} set to {}", field, value)` likewise), so a begins-with anchor alone cannot tell it from SQL — nothing but case can. The cost is the standard disclosed under-report of that gate: lowercase SQL (`format!("select {} from users", cols)`) is invisible to this rule. A SQL literal with no placeholder is not matched (nothing is being spliced in), and neither is a `format!` whose template carries no SQL statement keyword. That placeholder-free case is the sibling `sql/update-no-where`/`sql/delete-no-where` turf instead: a COMPLETE whole-table statement with nothing spliced in is a different defect (it runs on every row) reported at a different severity, and the two rules partition the line rather than both reporting it — this one needs a placeholder, those require its absence. The partition extends to the FILE SET: this rule excludes migration paths through the same `${test-paths-migrations}` vocabulary those siblings use — a migration interpolating an identifier into a schema statement is the canonical legitimate dynamic SQL, with nothing request-derived in reach. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-sql-format-interpolation-ok`.

A tainted-source access (request body/query/params/headers, `searchParams`, `process.argv`) and a dangerous sink (`eval`, `new Function`, `exec`/`spawn`, raw SQL, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `.innerHTML`) both appear in the same function — this is a coarse v1 check (source+sink co-occurrence, not real dataflow), so confirm the value is actually tainted here. Kept at `warning`, not `critical`: co-occurrence is an approximation of dataflow, not proof of it, and `critical` is reserved for matchers that can prove their claim — treat a hit as a lead to confirm, not a confirmed exploit. For a SQL sink, parameterize the query (prepared/parameterized statement API) — never escape or interpolate the tainted value into the SQL string. For a shell/process-exec sink, use `execFile`/`spawn` with an args array, not a shell-string `exec()` with string concatenation. For a DOM/HTML sink, use `textContent` (not `innerHTML`) for plain text, or a vetted HTML-sanitizer library if HTML must be inserted — never raw `innerHTML` with tainted input. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-taint-flow-ok`.

`eval(...)` called with a non-literal argument, or `new Function(...)` used at all (even with only literal arguments — constructing a function from a string at runtime still defeats CSP's `script-src` and is invisible to every static analyzer downstream, so it is a code smell worth surfacing regardless) — building and executing code from a runtime string is one of the highest-risk sinks in JS: if any part of that string can be influenced by user input, it's arbitrary code execution. Avoid dynamic code construction; use a plain function/lookup table/JSON.parse instead. Note: `security/taint-flow` already covers `eval` when a request-derived source co-occurs in the same function, `.ts`/`.tsx` only; this rule is source-free (fires on the construct itself, not just a proven-tainted case) and also covers `.js`/`.jsx`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a sandboxed plugin-eval with no user-controlled input) with `// zzop-eval-dynamic-code-ok`.

A method PROVEN by the parser's projected call-site channel to use a process-exec API — a `Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)` call spelled as that fixed platform chain, or a `new ProcessBuilder(...)` construction — also builds SOME string by concatenating an identifier onto a literal (`"..." + ident`; that half stays LEXICAL and is where this finding anchors). The exec witness used to be the BARE WORD `exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, which a local variable, field or unrelated method named `exec` satisfied just as well; the projected site retires that false-positive class, and the trade is disclosed rather than discovered: an exec reached through a VARIABLE (`Runtime rt = Runtime.getRuntime(); rt.exec(cmd)`, or a `ProcessBuilder` held in `pb` and started later) is not a resolvable spelling and is no longer evidence, and a file this engine cannot parse projects no sites at all — this rule is silent in both places where the bare-word version fired, and that silence is absence of evidence, never a clean bill. Between the two halves this is STILL a co-occurrence heuristic, not dataflow: nothing links the concatenated string to the command that gets executed (the two may be unrelated statements in the same method). When they are connected, and the concatenated part is request-derived, it is command injection. Cross-language siblings under the same concept name: the TypeScript sibling `security/shell-exec-interpolation` is `critical` because `exec`/`execSync` hand their whole command string to a shell; `Runtime.exec(String)` tokenizes on whitespace WITHOUT a shell, so a request-derived part injects extra argv tokens — or the program name itself — never shell syntax, which alongside the co-occurrence uncertainty above is why this rule is `warning`. The Rust sibling `security/command-and-interpolation` holds the same standing for its argv-direct `Command::new`. Pass arguments as an array element per token and validate/allow-list any user-controlled part. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-cmd-injection-ok`.

One Rust function PROVEN by the parser's projected call-site channel to construct an OS process (a `Command::new(...)` call, in its `std::process::`-qualified, `process::`-qualified or bare spelling — each kept as written) ALSO builds a string with a `format!`/`write!`/`writeln!` macro (that half stays LEXICAL and is where this finding anchors; the structural witness retires the string/comment false-fire class of the old regex, at a disclosed cost: a construction this engine cannot parse, or one reached through an aliased path, projects no site and the rule is silent there — absence of evidence, never a clean bill) — if that string reaches the PROGRAM NAME (`Command::new(formatted)`) or is routed through a shell (`Command::new("sh").arg("-c").arg(formatted)`) with a request-derived value, that is command injection. A formatted string passed as an ordinary `.arg(...)` is NOT: `Command::new` spawns the program directly with an argv array and no shell ever parses the string, so the worst an argument-position value enables is argument/option injection against the called program — real exposure, but not command injection, and the reason the TypeScript sibling `security/shell-exec-interpolation` (whose matched `exec` string IS shell-interpreted) is `critical` while this rule is not. `-and-` is literal here: this is CO-OCCURRENCE within one function body, not proof that the interpolated string is the one that gets executed (the two may be unrelated statements), which is why it is `warning` and not `critical` — same standing as the Java sibling `security/cmd-injection`. Scope boundary, stated honestly: a `String`+`&str` CONCATENATION is deliberately not matched. This rule used to claim it, and could not have it — Rust's `&str` implements no `Add`, so the `"literal" + expr` shape the arm spelled does not compile in any Rust program, while the forms that DO compile put `.to_string()` or a `)` between the quote and the `+`. The only lines that arm could reach were ones whose ESCAPED quotes made the regex mis-read where the literal ended, so it produced false positives and never coverage; it was removed rather than widened, because the macro arm already covers the interpolation this rule is named for. Pass every argument as its own `.arg(value)` rather than building one shell string, do not route through `sh -c`, and validate or allow-list any caller-supplied part. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-command-and-interpolation-ok`.

A dynamic segment (a template-literal `${...}` or a string-concatenation `+`) is spliced directly into `exec`/`execSync`'s shell-command-string argument — the shell interprets that whole string, so any dynamic part reaching it is command injection, whether or not this rule can prove it's request-derived (see boundary note below). Use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argv array instead — arguments passed as separate array elements are never shell-interpreted, which is exactly why this rule does not fire on `execFile`/`spawn` calls. Matched shapes are child_process-scoped TWICE over: the lexical arm still requires a bare/destructured `exec(...)`/`execSync(...)` call or a `child_process.`/`childProcess.`/`cp.` member spelling, AND the line must carry a parser-projected `process-exec` call site — the producer resolves the callee against this file's own `child_process`/`node:child_process` import (or top-level `require`) bindings, so a RegExp's own `pattern.exec(...)`, an unrelated helper named `exec`, or the same spelling inside a string literal or comment is structurally not a site and never fires. The structural gate's cost is disclosed rather than discovered: a file this engine cannot parse (degraded), or an exec reached through a binding the producer cannot resolve (a re-exported wrapper, a dynamic `import()`, an aliasing the module doc of the TypeScript producer excludes), projects no site and this rule is silent there where the pure regex used to fire — absence of evidence, never a clean bill. Boundary: `security/taint-flow` also flags `exec`/`execSync` as a sink, but only when a request-derived source co-occurs in the same `.ts`/`.tsx` function; this rule needs no source, fires on the interpolation shape alone, and also covers plain `.js` files — treat the two as complementary, not redundant. Cross-language siblings under the same concept name, deliberately weaker: Java `security/cmd-injection` and Rust `security/command-and-interpolation` are both `warning`, because the APIs they match (`Runtime.exec`'s whitespace tokenization, `Command::new`'s direct argv spawn) hand nothing to a shell — this rule alone is `critical` because `exec`/`execSync`'s command string IS handed to a shell, so a dynamic segment needs no further conditions to become injection. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-shell-exec-interpolation-ok`.

`DocumentBuilderFactory`/`SAXParserFactory.newInstance()` with no recognized XXE guard in the same method — a default-configured XML parser resolves external entities, so crafted XML can read local files, perform SSRF, or exhaust memory. Set `disallow-doctype-decl` to `true`; `FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING` alone does NOT disable external entity resolution and is not sufficient on its own. If DOCTYPEs are genuinely required, set both `external-general-entities` and `external-parameter-entities` to `false` instead. Each recognized guard pattern silences this finding independently (any one alone is enough to veto it). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-xxe-no-guard-ok`.

A `new ObjectInputStream` construction and a `readObject(` call CO-OCCUR in this Java method — TWO INDEPENDENT patterns (`new\s+ObjectInputStream` and `\breadObject\s*\(`), not one dotted `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` chain — that dotted shape is never matched as such, and nothing links the call's receiver to the constructed stream, so a `readObject(` on an unrelated object satisfies the second pattern just as well — the regex is receiverless, so even the DECLARATION of a custom `private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)` serialization hook matches it. No order is required either, and the reported line is the `readObject(` one, which is the trigger. When they ARE connected, Java's native deserialization invokes arbitrary code paths (gadget chains), so deserializing an attacker-controlled byte stream can lead to remote code execution. Kept at `warning` because this local analysis can't prove the deserialized payload is attacker-reachable — treat it as CRITICAL wherever the input actually comes from a request body/query/header/upload. Use JSON/Protobuf instead, or validate the stream with an allow-list `ObjectInputFilter`. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-unsafe-deserialization-ok`.

This line uses a template-engine syntax that emits UNescaped HTML: EJS `<%- %>`, Handlebars `{{{ }}}` triple-stache, or Mustache `{{& }}` — if any interpolated value is user-influenced, this is reflected/stored server-side XSS. Use the escaped output form instead (EJS `<%= %>`, Handlebars/Mustache `{{ }}`), or route the value through a vetted sanitizer when intentional raw HTML is actually required. Sibling boundary: `browser/unsafe-html-sink` catches the client-side DOM-sink half of this class (`innerHTML` assignment in browser code); this rule catches the server-side template-engine half that produces the HTML in the first place — complementary, not overlapping. Scoped to template file extensions only (`.ejs`/`.hbs`/`.handlebars`/`.mustache`/`.njk`/`.nunjucks`), since these tokens only mean "unescaped output" inside a template file. (Pug's buffered `!= expr` form is deliberately NOT covered: it is lexically indistinguishable from Pug/Nunjucks's loose-inequality operator `!=`, so flagging it would false-fire on every `a != b` conditional — a never-guess omission, not an oversight.) Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-template-unescaped-output-ok` — but note `//` is not a comment in EJS/Handlebars/Mustache/Nunjucks, so an inline marker there renders as literal page output, and inline suppression isn't clean there — prefer the config-level disable (hint below).

A `res.send`/`res.write`/`res.end` call co-occurs with request input (`req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body`/`req.headers`) AND an HTML-shaped marker (a literal opening tag like `<div>`/`<html>`, or a `Content-Type: text/html` header) in the same function, with no sanitizer call anywhere in it — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not a proof that the request value actually reaches the HTML output (same honesty as `db/multi-write-no-tx`'s documented approximation): it flags the shape, not a traced data flow. Escape/sanitize request-derived values before splicing them into HTML, set an explicit `application/json` content type for pure API responses, or use a template engine with auto-escaping instead of building markup by hand. Sibling boundary: `security/taint-flow` also does source+sink co-occurrence for `.ts`/`.tsx`, but its sink list does not include `res.send`/`res.write`/`res.end` — this rule covers exactly the class taint-flow misses, and also runs on plain `.js`/`.cjs`/`.mjs` files taint-flow doesn't scan. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-html-response-from-request-ok`.

A string literal that opens or closes an HTML tag (`"
"`, `""`, ...) is concatenated with a non-literal (`+ someVar` / `someVar +`) in a file that also mentions a `res`/`response`/content-type-`text/html` server-response context — building HTML by concatenating a variable into tag markup is an injection sink if that variable is user-influenced. Use a template engine with auto-escaping, or a sanitizer, instead of hand-assembling markup. Kept `warning` and deployed-surface-excluded because this is shape-only and FP-prone (logging strings, test fixtures, non-response string building all read the same way to a regex) — the `require_file` gate on a response/content-type mention is there specifically to bias this toward real server-response context rather than firing on every HTML-shaped concatenation in the repo. Sibling boundary: `html-response-from-request` needs the request-input+HTML-marker co-occurrence inside one function; this rule needs neither — it fires on the concatenation shape alone, so treat the two as complementary. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-dangerous-html-concat-ok`.

A filesystem call (`fs`/`fsp.*`, `readFile`/`writeFile`), request input (`req.params`/`req.query`/`req.body`), and a `path.join(...)` call all appear in the same function — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the request-derived value actually flows into the joined path, but when it does: an unvalidated `..` segment lets an attacker escape the intended directory (path traversal). Reject `..` segments, or verify the resolved path stays under the base directory. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-path-traversal-ok`.

rules._note: Rule id intentionally keeps its `java-` prefix: dropping it to `path-traversal` would collide with this pack's existing JS `path-traversal` rule (the Java `new File(...)` + `request.getParameter(...)` shape is distinct from the JS fs+path.join shape). The prefix earns its keep as a disambiguator.
rules.message: `new File(...)` is constructed in a method that also reads `request.getParameter(...)` — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not proof the parameter reaches the path: the two patterns may match unrelated statements in the same method, and nothing here checks order or dataflow (a `new File(...)` on a constant path in a method that reads an unrelated parameter fires just the same). It is deliberately weaker evidence than its TypeScript sibling `path-traversal`, which requires a third co-occurring `path.join(...)`. When they ARE connected, an unvalidated parameter flowing into the path lets an attacker escape the intended directory and read/write files outside it. Reject `..` segments, or resolve and compare against the base directory before use. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-java-path-traversal-ok`.

An outbound HTTP call (`fetch`/`axios`/`got`) is made in a function that also reads `req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body` — if that value becomes part of the URL, the server can be made to request attacker-chosen hosts (SSRF), reaching internal services or a metadata endpoint. Validate the target against an allow-list of hosts. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-ssrf-user-url-ok`.

`redirect(...)` is called in a function that also reads `req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body` — an unchecked request-derived target lets an attacker send victims to an arbitrary external site (open redirect), a common phishing/OAuth-token-theft vector. Validate the target against an allow-list of known internal paths. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-open-redirect-ok`.

`sendFile`/`download` is called with a `req.params`/`req.query`/`req.body`-derived path — the sibling `path-traversal` rule catches `fs`/`path.join` reads built from request input in the same shape, but does not cover Express's file-serving APIs (`res.sendFile`/`res.download`) directly, so this rule fills that gap. An unvalidated `..` segment lets an attacker read arbitrary files off disk via path traversal. Reject `..` segments, or resolve the path and confirm it stays under the intended base directory, before passing it in. v1 is kept honest rather than clever: a same-line `path.basename(...)` call vetoes the finding by simple textual co-presence, not by proving it actually wraps the request-derived argument — a real sanitizer elsewhere in the function is not detected. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-sendfile-from-request-ok`.

A digest the PARSER witnessed being constructed with a broken algorithm (MD5 or SHA-1) sits on a line that also names a credential (`password`/`passwd`/`pwd`) — those digests are too cheap to resist offline brute force at billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs. Use bcrypt with a cost factor of at least 10, or argon2id/scrypt at OWASP-recommended memory/parallelism parameters. WHAT COUNTS AS A HASH moved from a text regex to the parser's projected call-site channel on 2026-08-03, and the reach moved in three directions worth naming rather than discovering. It is NARROWER and more honest: the old arms matched the bare word `md5`/`sha1` anywhere on a line, so a variable, a parameter, an error message or a project's own helper named `md5` satisfied them exactly as well as a real digest construction — none of those fires now, and neither does an algorithm named only inside a string literal or a comment, because a mention is not a construction. It is WIDER by language: one rule covers TypeScript/JavaScript (`crypto.createHash`), Python (`hashlib`), Java (`MessageDigest.getInstance`), C# (`MD5.Create`/`HashAlgorithm.Create`), Go (`crypto/md5` and its siblings) and Rust (the `md5`/`sha1`/`sha2` crates), each with that platform's own spellings. And it is narrower in a way that costs recall, disclosed rather than discovered: a digest whose ALGORITHM the source does not spell at the site (`createHash(algoVar)`, `hashlib.new(name)`, `MessageDigest.getInstance(algo)`) carries no algorithm at all — never-guess — so this rule says nothing there, and the same holds for a file this engine cannot parse, for a hashing package no producer claims, and for a construction whose credential word sits on a different line. Silence here is absence of evidence, never a clean bill. The credential-word half stays LEXICAL and stays a CO-OCCURRENCE: it proves the two appear on one line, not that this digest hashes that password — which is why this rule is `warning` and not `critical`, and why a line that REJECTS a weak algorithm while naming a credential reads the same to it. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-weak-password-hash-ok` (`# zzop-weak-password-hash-ok` in Python).

bcrypt invoked with a SINGLE-DIGIT cost factor passed AFTER the value being hashed (`bcrypt.hash(pw, 8)`, `bcrypt.hashSync(pw, 4)`) — each increment doubles the work, so a single-digit cost is orders of magnitude below the current recommendation and falls to offline brute force on commodity GPUs. Use a cost factor of at least 10; the unit is bcrypt-specific and is NOT a scrypt/argon2 parameter. This arm shipped inside `security/weak-password-hash` until the 2026-08-03 call-site migration and was split out rather than carried along, because it is a different claim about a different thing: its sibling now judges WHICH DIGEST the parser witnessed being constructed, while a bcrypt cost factor is a numeric ARGUMENT to an adaptive hash that is itself the recommended answer — there is no digest construction to witness, so the structural channel has nothing to say here and the check stays lexical. Being lexical it is a one-line shape match, with the limits that implies: a cost passed through a constant (`bcrypt.hash(pw, COST)`) or configured elsewhere is invisible to it, and it reads a literal digit only. One more limit, disclosed rather than left to be discovered: the cost must sit in an argument position AFTER another argument, so every call whose cost is the FIRST argument is unmatchable — the salt-first family (`bcrypt.genSalt(4, cb)`, `bcrypt.genSaltSync(4)`, and the nested `bcrypt.hashSync(pw, bcrypt.genSaltSync(4))`) stays silent today no matter how low the cost. What decides is the POSITION, not the argument count: `genSaltSync(saltRounds, 4)` does fire. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-bcrypt-cost-too-low-ok`.

`Math.random()` is used on the same line as a token/otp/nonce/session-id/secret-shaped identifier — it's a predictable PRNG, not cryptographically secure, so a value generated this way can be guessed or brute-forced. Use `crypto.randomBytes(n).toString('hex')` or `crypto.randomUUID()`. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-weak-token-random-ok`.

`new Random()` is used on the same line as a token/session/otp/nonce-shaped identifier — `java.util.Random` is a predictable PRNG, not cryptographically secure, so a value generated this way can be predicted or brute-forced. Use `java.security.SecureRandom` instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-weak-random-ok`.

Weak/deprecated cryptography in use — MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision attacks (forgeable signatures/certificates), DES/RC4 are brute-forceable or biased, and ECB mode leaks plaintext structure across blocks. Use SHA-256 or stronger for hashing and AES-GCM for encryption; for passwords specifically use bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2 (a fast hash is the wrong tool even at SHA-256). Suppress a vetted non-security use (e.g. a legacy-interop checksum) with `// zzop-weak-crypto-ok`.

A secret/token/signature/hmac/api-key-shaped identifier is compared with `===`/`!==` — equality operators short-circuit on the first differing byte, so the comparison time itself can leak a timing signal about the value to an attacker positioned to measure it. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual(...)` on fixed-length buffers instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-timing-unsafe-compare-ok`.

TLS certificate/hostname verification is disabled (a trust-all `X509TrustManager`, `ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER`, or a `setHostnameVerifier` lambda always returning `true`) — accepts any certificate for any host, so the app can't detect a man-in-the-middle. Use the default (or a properly validating custom) trust manager/verifier. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-trust-all-tls-ok`.

`jwt.sign(...)` is called where `expiresIn` never appears in the same function — a token with no expiry is valid forever, so a leak (logs, XSS, a compromised client) can be replayed indefinitely. Pass `{ expiresIn: '...' }` (or set `exp` in the payload) so tokens expire. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-jwt-no-expiry-ok`.

`algorithm(s): 'none'` appears in a JWT-related file — `alg: none` turns signature verification off entirely, so a caller can mint an arbitrary token that validates with any payload it wants. There is no legitimate production use of this algorithm. Remove `none` from the allowed/signing algorithm list and use a real algorithm (`HS256`/`RS256`/...), pinning `algorithms` explicitly on the verifying side too so a future token can't downgrade itself. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a local test harness that intentionally exercises the none-alg attack) with `// zzop-jwt-none-algorithm-ok`.

`ignoreExpiration: true` or `verify: false` appears in a file that imports a JWT library (`jsonwebtoken`/`jose`/a `jwt` specifier) — either option turns off a check `jwt.verify` exists to perform: `ignoreExpiration: true` accepts an expired token, `verify: false` accepts one with no signature check at all (an outright auth bypass). The require-file gate on a JWT-library import is load-bearing here: bare `verify: false` also appears in plenty of unrelated configs (bundlers, linters, ...), and without the gate this rule would fire on those too. Remove the option (or set it to the safe default) so `jwt.verify` performs its normal checks. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-jwt-verify-bypass-ok`.

CORS origin set to `*` (a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, `origin: '*'`, or a Rust framework's allow-any idiom) — lets any website make cross-origin requests to this endpoint, defeating same-origin protection. Return a specific allow-listed origin instead, especially on endpoints that accept cookies or auth headers. The Rust arms match the dominant idioms by their own spelling rather than the wire header: tower-http's `.allow_origin(Any)` (any path-qualified spelling of `Any`), actix-web's `.allow_any_origin()`, and the typed constant `ACCESS_CONTROL_ALLOW_ORIGIN` paired with a `"*"` literal on the same line. Spellings beyond those — a wildcard reached through a variable, a config file, or a framework not named here — are NOT seen; for them only the literal header text arm applies. A wildcard is legitimate for a purely public, credential-less API (no cookies/auth headers involved) — suppress that case with `// zzop-cors-wildcard-ok` rather than "fixing" it.

`credentials: true` appears in a file that also configures `origin: '*'` — the pairing is FILE-level, not object-level: the two keys are matched anywhere in the same file, so they may belong to two unrelated config objects (a wildcard-origin public CORS block and a separate credentialed one) and still fire. Browsers actually REJECT (refuse to expose the response for) a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` combined with credentials, so this exact configuration is broken/non-functional rather than exploitable as written. The real risk: to "fix" the breakage, code often reflects the request's `Origin` header back with `credentials: true` still set — that treats any origin as trusted and IS the actual vulnerability. Return a specific allow-listed origin (never `*`, never an echoed `Origin`) whenever `credentials: true` is set. Both matched keys are JS OBJECT-LITERAL shapes (`credentials: true`, `origin: '*'`), not wire-header values, so this rule deliberately scans JS/TS only — Rust/other-language CORS config is builder-call shaped and is not judged here (unlike the sibling `cors-wildcard`/`csp-weak-or-disabled`, whose header-value arms do scan `.rs`). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-cors-credentials-wildcard-ok`.

`credentials: true` co-occurs on one line with `origin: true` (cors()'s reflect-any-origin mode) or `origin: req.headers...` (manually echoing the request's Origin header) — either shape treats any origin as trusted while allowing cookies/credentials, which is the actual exploitable CORS misconfiguration (unlike a literal `'*'`, which browsers reject alongside credentials). Sibling boundary: `cors-wildcard`/`cors-credentials-wildcard` cover the literal `'*'` shape; this rule covers the REFLECTION shape those two miss. Return a specific allow-listed origin instead of reflecting the request's origin. Known limitation, not desired behavior: this is a single-line co-occurrence check, so a multi-line CORS options object (each key on its own line) is missed — see the pinned fixture documenting this gap. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-cors-reflected-origin-credentials-ok`.

Content-Security-Policy is explicitly turned off or weakened: Helmet's `contentSecurityPolicy: false`, a `Content-Security-Policy` header value containing `unsafe-inline`, or a `default-src` directive containing a wildcard `*` — CSP is the browser's last line of defense against XSS once a payload has already been injected, so disabling/weakening it removes a mitigation that has nothing to do with whether the injection itself is possible. Keep a restrictive policy: enable Helmet's default CSP (or a hand-configured one) instead of `false`, drop `unsafe-inline` in favor of nonces/hashes, and scope `default-src`/`script-src` to specific allow-listed origins instead of `*`. The two header-value arms are wire-header shapes, so this rule also scans `.rs` (a Rust service setting the literal `Content-Security-Policy` header is judged exactly like a JS one); the `helmet-csp-false` arm is a JS-library option key and is silent in `.rs` by nature — arm-level silence in one language, not rule-level silence. Kept at `warning` because this is a mitigation-ABSENCE rule (defense-in-depth), not proof of an exploitable injection by itself. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-csp-weak-or-disabled-ok`.

A cookie is set (`res.cookie`/`setCookie`/`cookies.set`) without `httpOnly` in the same function — a session/auth cookie without it is readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug becomes full session theft. Add `{ httpOnly: true }` (plus `secure`/`sameSite` as appropriate). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-insecure-cookie-ok`.

A raw error object is sent directly to the client (`res.status(5xx).send/json(err)`, or Hono's `c.json(err)`) — errors often carry stack traces, file paths, or internal config that help an attacker map the system. Log server-side and send a generic message (e.g. `{ error: 'Internal server error' }`) instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-error-leak-to-client-ok`.

A stack-trace call (`printStackTrace()`, `getStackTrace()`) and an HTTP-response token (`getWriter()`, `ResponseEntity`, `@ResponseBody`, `HttpServletResponse`) both appear in the same method — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the trace is written to the response (a `printStackTrace()` that goes to stderr in a method that merely mentions `HttpServletResponse` fires too). When the trace does reach the client, it exposes internal class names and file paths. Log server-side and return a generic error body instead. (A custom exception's `.getMessage()` — a curated message string, not a stack trace — is deliberately NOT flagged, to match this rule's stack-trace-exposure scope.) Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-stacktrace-to-response-ok`.

A token/JWT-shaped value is written to `localStorage` — readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS bug anywhere on the origin can exfiltrate it with no further exploitation. Default fix: store it in an `httpOnly` cookie with `sameSite` set, plus CSRF-token protection. This isn't a full fix either — cookies reintroduce CSRF risk (mitigated by `sameSite`/CSRF tokens), and an active XSS bug can still ride an existing cookie session in-place — but it does stop direct token theft/exfiltration. Accepted alternative: an in-memory access token with a rotating refresh token, or a Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) pattern. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-localstorage-jwt-ok`.

`req.body` (or a spread of it) passed directly into a database write (`create`/`update`/`upsert`/`updateMany`) — an attacker can set any field the model accepts (role, isAdmin, price, ownerId, ...) that the handler never intended to expose. Whitelist the fields you accept, or use a validated DTO. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-mass-assignment-ok`.
